I believe we must maintain a robust 18% Infrastructure investment to support remote work and connectivity, while strategically allocating 9% to Economic Development to prevent the community from becoming a "residential dormitory" and 8% to Green Spaces to preserve our quality of life. This holistic "Retention Loop" approach balances immediate human capital needs with the long-term economic sustainability required to keep our community thriving.

Based on the committee's evolution, I would recommend a final allocation of **35% Education, 30% Healthcare, 18% Infrastructure, 12% Economic Development, and 5% Green Spaces**. This split prioritizes the retention crisis by heavily investing in our schools and health, while using Infrastructure and Economic Development to create the "destination" quality of life that keeps our talent here. However, I would strongly advise the decision-maker to cap Green Spaces at 5% to prevent the community from becoming a sterile commuter hub, ensuring that our investment in people is the primary driver of our future, not just our scenery.

I believe we have to treat this $10 million grant as a strategic investment in our community's survival, specifically targeting the brain drain that is threatening our future. My view is that we must anchor our budget at 35% for Education to immediately address the dip in test scores and teacher turnover, but we cannot support that investment in isolation. I advocate for a holistic approach where we protect Healthcare at 30% to keep families healthy, and we maintain a robust 15-18% for Infrastructure and Economic Development to ensure our community isn't just a place to live, but a place with jobs and connectivity that makes staying worthwhile.

After extensive debate, I have settled on a final allocation of 35% Education, 30% Healthcare, 18% Infrastructure, 6% Economic Development, and 11% Green Spaces, viewing this as a holistic "Survival Kit" that prioritizes the retention of our current workforce by addressing the root causes of the brain drain. I have evolved from seeing green spaces as a luxury to recognizing them as a critical retention subsidy, and I now firmly believe that infrastructure and economic development must be lean and targeted—specifically as "Local Workforce Development"—rather than speculative expansion, to ensure we build a self-sustaining ecosystem where our staff can live, work, and thrive without commuting.

Based on the data regarding declining test scores and teacher turnover, I would recommend a budget allocation of **35% Education, 30% Healthcare, 18% Infrastructure, 6% Economic Development, and 11% Green Spaces**. This split prioritizes the "crumbling foundation" of our community by anchoring the budget in Education and Healthcare to directly address the root causes of the retention crisis, while using Infrastructure and Green Spaces as essential retention tools rather than speculative luxuries. By maintaining a lean Economic Development focus on internal workforce development, we ensure fiscal sustainability without overextending the town's capacity, creating a self-sustaining ecosystem where we invest in the people we already have to make living here viable.

I believe we have to fundamentally shift our strategy from trying to attract new people to keeping the ones we already have, which means Education has to be the anchor of our budget. I’ve moved away from the idea that we can just build our way out of this with fancy infrastructure or economic development; instead, I see the crumbling foundation of our schools as the root cause of our problems. To fix that, we need a "total package" that combines a strong education system with essential healthcare and livable green spaces, while keeping our economic development lean and focused on internal workforce support rather than speculative growth.

This holistic approach ensures we are not just maintaining the status quo, but actively building a self-sustaining ecosystem that retains our current workforce while attracting the next generation of talent.
